notes.meaning: The evil spirit gave one last violent attack as it was forced to leave, throwing the young boy into convulsions. The boy lay so still that the crowd thought he was dead. Satan often tries to do the greatest harm right before his power is broken by Christ.

Jesus reached out, took the boy by the hand, and lifted him up fully restored. His gentle touch proved that the boy was alive and completely healed. Jesus always completes the work of deliverance He begins.

Once they were inside away from the crowd, the disciples asked Jesus why their own attempt to cast out the demon had failed. They had successfully driven out demons before, so this defeat puzzled and embarrassed them. Their question showed they needed to learn where real spiritual power comes from.

Jesus told them that this stubborn kind of demon could only be driven out through earnest prayer. Power over dark spirits comes from continual dependence on God rather than past success or personal ability. Believers must stay closely connected to God when facing difficult spiritual battles.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The earliest and best Greek manuscripts leave out the words and fasting, suggesting they were added by later copyists to highlight physical self-denial.

notes.meaning: Jesus and His followers traveled quietly through the region of Galilee. He kept their journey secret from the crowds so He could focus on preparing the Twelve for what lay ahead. He chose quiet instruction over public miracles during this crucial time.

Jesus explained to them that He would be handed over to wicked men who would kill Him, but He would rise from the dead three days later. He spoke of His death and resurrection—rising back to life—to prepare them for the cross. Knowing God's plan ahead of time was meant to strengthen their trust when tragedy struck.

The disciples did not grasp what He meant because they still expected Him to set up an earthly kingdom right away. They were also afraid to ask for an explanation because they feared hearing more painful news. Their grief and confusion kept them from welcoming the truth about His coming sacrifice.

After arriving at their home base in Capernaum, Jesus asked the disciples what they had been talking about on the road. He already knew their thoughts, but He asked to help them face their own motives. Honest reflection before the Lord exposes pride that we might otherwise hide.

The disciples stayed completely quiet because they were ashamed to admit what they had been doing. While traveling, they had argued about which of them would hold the highest position in the Messiah's kingdom. Their silence showed that their consciences convicted them of their selfish ambition.

Jesus sat down like a teacher and gave them the true standard of rank in the kingdom of God. Anyone who wants to be first must choose the lowest place and serve everyone else. True greatness is measured by humble service rather than power over others.

Jesus brought a young child into the center of the group and wrapped His arms around him. In those days, children had no social power or status. By embracing someone small and helpless, Jesus gave a visual picture of how to treat the lowly.

Receiving and caring for a humble person in the name of Jesus is the same as welcoming Jesus Himself. Furthermore, welcoming Christ means welcoming the Father who sent Him. God measures our love for Him by how we treat the weakest members of His family.

John mentioned that they had tried to stop a man who was driving out demons in Jesus' name because he was not part of their immediate traveling group. The disciples thought ministry should be limited strictly to their own circle. John's concern revealed lingering jealousy and a narrow view of God's work.

Jesus told them never to hinder such a person from doing good. Anyone who performs a mighty deed using the name of Jesus will not easily turn around and speak evil of Him. God often works through people outside our immediate group to advance His kingdom.

Anyone who does not oppose Christ's work is actually helping His cause. Jesus teaches His followers to take a generous view of other workers rather than treating them as rivals. We should rejoice whenever the power of evil is broken, even if it happens outside our fellowship.

Even the smallest act of kindness, such as giving a cup of water to a disciple because they belong to Christ, will receive a sure reward. The Lord notices and honors every deed done out of love for Him. No service offered in His name is ever wasted or forgotten.

Leading a humble believer into sin brings terrible guilt. Jesus warns that drowning in the sea with a heavy millstone tied around the neck would be better than facing God's punishment for causing a little one to fall away. Protecting the faith of fellow Christians is an urgent duty for every believer.

Jesus uses strong figurative language to show that believers must cut off whatever causes them to stumble into sin, even if it feels as dear as a hand. Hell, called Gehenna, is a place of unquenchable fire where the unrepentant face final ruin. It is far better to give up precious worldly pleasures now than to lose everything in eternal judgment.

Quoting the prophet Isaiah, this verse portrays the unending misery of hell. The gnawing worm pictures inward agony and remorse of conscience, while the fire pictures outward punishment. Refusing to turn from sin leads to a ruin that never ends.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The oldest Greek manuscripts omit this verse here, indicating that scribes copied it from verse 48 to complete the pattern.

notes.meaning: Jesus repeats His warning using the foot, teaching that Christians must turn away from places and habits that lead them into evil. Losing what seems useful in this life is nothing compared to the tragedy of being cast into hell. True discipleship calls for decisive action against temptation.

The warning is stated once more to stress the certainty and permanence of eternal loss. Sinners who refuse God's mercy will find no relief from inner remorse or outward judgment. God's repeated warnings are meant to turn people toward repentance before it is too late.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Early Greek manuscripts lack this verse, showing it was inserted by copyists from the parallel statement in verse 48.

notes.meaning: Even something as precious and sensitive as an eye must be plucked out metaphorically if it feeds sinful desires. Entering the kingdom of God with worldly losses is far better than keeping everything and ending up in hell. Disciples must guard what they look at and cherish above all else.

Here Jesus quotes Isaiah to describe hell as a place where the worm never dies and the fire is never put out. This terrible language pictures complete corruption and unending distress for those who reject God. Taking sin lightly ignores the terrifying reality of divine judgment.

Just as ancient sacrifices were seasoned with salt under God's law, every follower of Christ must pass through the purifying fire of trials and self-denial. This fiery seasoning burns away selfishness and preserves the soul in true holiness. Facing hardships for Christ refines our character so that our lives become pleasing offerings to God.

Salt is valuable for seasoning and preserving, but if it loses its saltiness, it becomes entirely useless. Jesus urges His disciples to keep spiritual purity and grace within their hearts so they can season the world around them. Instead of competing for rank, they must live in peace and harmony with one another.
